Significant (<italic>p</italic> < 0.05) values are indicated in bold.</p></fn></table-wrap-foot></table-wrap></sec><sec id="emi70430-sec-0010" disp-level="2"><label>3.2.</label><title>Beta‐Diversity</title><p>PERMANOVA revealed that disturbance history, major pulse, time and all their interaction significantly affected community composition (Table <xref rid="emi70430-supitem-0001" ref-type="supplementary-material">S2</xref>). PERMDISP showed that, across all time points, multivariate dispersion differed significantly among disturbance‐history treatments, between major‐pulse treatments and among sampling times (Table <xref rid="emi70430-supitem-0001" ref-type="supplementary-material">S3</xref>). Additionally, PCoA ordination indicates that time was a major factor structuring community composition with an increase in beta‐diversity over time (Figure <xref rid="emi70430-fig-0003" ref-type="fig">3</xref>, Figure <xref rid="emi70430-supitem-0001" ref-type="supplementary-material">S4a–c</xref>). Variation among replicate communities was also evident in their taxonomic composition at the final sampling day. Relative abundances at the phylum level showed distinct compositional differences among replicates within each disturbance‐history treatment (Figure <xref rid="emi70430-supitem-0001" ref-type="supplementary-material">S3</xref>).</p><fig id="emi70430-fig-0003" position="float"><?disp-level 3?><label>FIGURE 3</label><caption><p>Principal coordinate analysis (PCoA) showing differences in bacterial community composition (based on Aitchison distances of 16S rRNA gene amplicon sequencing data) for no major pulse compared to major pulse treatments. The colour gradient indicates time (dark shades indicate early and lighter shades later days in the experiment).</p></caption><alternatives><graphic xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" content-type="image" id="jats-graphic-7" xlink:href="EMI-28-e70430-g004.webp"><?cloudpmc-path blobs/6241/13616742/4f6ac3213b4a/EMI-28-e70430-g004.webp?><?cloudpmc-bucket cdn?><?image-server-status NEED_LOADING?><?original-height 763?><?original-width 1064?><?scaled-height 763?><?scaled-width 1064?></graphic><graphic xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" content-type="thumb" xlink:href="EMI-28-e70430-g004.gif"><?cloudpmc-path blobs/6241/13616742/e316c1a086c8/EMI-28-e70430-g004.gif?><?cloudpmc-bucket cdn?></graphic></alternatives></fig><p>We calculated pairwise Aitchison distances within each treatment and time point to quantify the divergence between replicates. Before the major pulse, pairwise Aitchison distances increased over time and slopes increased significantly more in both the long and short recovery treatments compared to the undisturbed control (Figure <xref rid="emi70430-fig-0004" ref-type="fig">4</xref>; Table <xref rid="emi70430-tbl-0002" ref-type="table">2</xref>), although the magnitude of these differences was relatively small. After the major pulse, Aitchison distances became flatter across treatments. There was a significant effect of disturbance history and the major pulse on Aitchison distance, as well as the interaction between the major pulse and disturbance history (Table <xref rid="emi70430-tbl-0002" ref-type="table">2</xref>). More specifically, in treatments with a disturbance history (both long and short recovery) Aitchison distances were higher in treatments receiving the major pulse compared to those not receiving it, while no such effect was visible in treatments without a disturbance history (Figure <xref rid="emi70430-fig-0004" ref-type="fig">4</xref>).</p><fig id="emi70430-fig-0004" position="float"><?disp-level 3?><label>FIGURE 4</label><caption><p>Pairwise Aitchison distance (dissimilarity between replicates) over time for each treatment: control (no disturbance history), long recovery treatment and short recovery treatment. Squares indicate samples collected before the major pulse on Day 27. Following the major pulse, filled circles represent treatments exposed to the pulse, whereas open circles represent treatments not exposed to the pulse. Solid and dashed lines represent GAM smoothers fitted to temporal trajectories for major pulse and no‐major pulse treatments, respectively; shaded areas indicate 95% confidence intervals. Blue and red shaded areas indicate the timing of the minor salinity pulses in the long and short recovery treatments, respectively.</p></caption><alternatives><graphic xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" content-type="image" id="jats-graphic-9" xlink:href="EMI-28-e70430-g003.webp"><?cloudpmc-path blobs/6241/13616742/9aff3fa9de75/EMI-28-e70430-g003.webp?><?cloudpmc-bucket cdn?><?image-server-status NEED_LOADING?><?original-height 1150?><?original-width 1064?><?scaled-height 1150?><?scaled-width 1064?></graphic><graphic xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" content-type="thumb" xlink:href="EMI-28-e70430-g003.gif"><?cloudpmc-path blobs/6241/13616742/ad2d5f8a8ea6/EMI-28-e70430-g003.gif?><?cloudpmc-bucket cdn?></graphic></alternatives></fig></sec><sec id="emi70430-sec-0011" disp-level="2"><label>3.3.</label><title>Null Modelling</title><p>Results from the null model analysis showed that NST values exceeded 0.5 across all treatments and at nearly all time points (Figure <xref rid="emi70430-fig-0005" ref-type="fig">5</xref>). Prior to the major pulse, NST increased significantly over time, and both disturbance history treatments exhibited higher NST values than the undisturbed control (Table <xref rid="emi70430-tbl-0002" ref-type="table">2</xref>). Following the major pulse, disturbance history remained associated with differences in NST (Table <xref rid="emi70430-tbl-0002" ref-type="table">2</xref>; Figure <xref rid="emi70430-fig-0005" ref-type="fig">5</xref>), and the pulse itself had a close to significant effect (<italic>p</italic> = 0.094). The interaction between disturbance history and the major pulse was significant only for the long recovery treatment, in which communities exposed to the major pulse displayed consistently higher NST values than those that did not receive the pulse (Figure <xref rid="emi70430-fig-0005" ref-type="fig">5</xref>; Table <xref rid="emi70430-tbl-0002" ref-type="table">2</xref>).</p><fig id="emi70430-fig-0005" position="float"><?disp-level 3?><label>FIGURE 5</label><caption><p>Normalized stochasticity ratio (NST; based on null modelling of pairwise Aitchison distances) over time for each treatment: control (no disturbance history), long recovery treatment and short recovery treatment. Squares indicate samples collected before the major pulse on Day 27. Following the major pulse, filled circles represent treatments exposed to the pulse, whereas open circles represent treatments not exposed to the pulse. Solid and dashed lines represent GAM smoothers fitted to temporal trajectories for major pulse and no‐major pulse treatments, respectively; shaded areas indicate 95% confidence intervals. Blue and red shaded areas indicate the timing of the minor salinity pulses in the long and short recovery treatments, respectively.</p></caption><alternatives><graphic xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" content-type="image" id="jats-graphic-11" xlink:href="EMI-28-e70430-g001.webp"><?cloudpmc-path blobs/6241/13616742/dc9ea58c63e2/EMI-28-e70430-g001.webp?><?cloudpmc-bucket cdn?><?image-server-status NEED_LOADING?><?original-height 1157?><?original-width 1064?><?scaled-height 1157?><?scaled-width 1064?></graphic><graphic xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" content-type="thumb" xlink:href="EMI-28-e70430-g001.gif"><?cloudpmc-path blobs/6241/13616742/8889b18dd3ee/EMI-28-e70430-g001.gif?><?cloudpmc-bucket cdn?></graphic></alternatives></fig></sec></sec><sec id="emi70430-sec-0012" disp-level="1"><label>4.</label><title>Discussion</title><p>We conducted a continuous‐culture experiment in which bacterial communities were exposed to repeated minor salinity pulses, followed, after different time lags, by a final major salinity pulse. We hypothesized that prior disturbance exposure would reduce microbial community sensitivity to later disturbances of the same type, and that the strength of this effect would diminish with increasing time between the previous and subsequent disturbance. Furthermore, we expected dissimilarity among replicate communities, and thus inferred stochasticity, to increase over time, but at a reduced rate during disturbance events.</p><p>Our study demonstrates that both the history and timing of prior disturbances shape bacterial community responses to a subsequent salinity pulse. In communities without a disturbance history (controls), the major salinity pulse disturbance decreased richness relative to communities that were not exposed to the pulse (Figure <xref rid="emi70430-fig-0002" ref-type="fig">2</xref>). Furthermore, richness in communities with a disturbance history (long and in particular short recovery) increased after the major pulse and even exceeded maximum richness of the control treatment. This result shows that legacy effects can buffer microbial communities against additional stress (Halbrook et al. <xref rid="emi70430-bib-0022" ref-type="bibr">2024</xref>), perhaps because frequent disturbances before the major pulse selected for stress‐tolerant or opportunistic taxa, enabling resistance to further species loss (Jurburg et al. <xref rid="emi70430-bib-0027" ref-type="bibr">2017</xref>; Peng et al. <xref rid="emi70430-bib-0038" ref-type="bibr">2024</xref>; Oram et al. <xref rid="emi70430-bib-0037" ref-type="bibr">2025</xref>). Although resistance and recovery were not directly quantified, this pattern suggests that frequent disturbances shortly before the major pulse preconditioned the community into a state that experienced reduced richness loss during the pulse and even an increase in richness afterwards (Allison and Martiny <xref rid="emi70430-bib-0004" ref-type="bibr">2008</xref>; Shade et al. <xref rid="emi70430-bib-0046" ref-type="bibr">2012</xref>; Zhou et al. <xref rid="emi70430-bib-0057" ref-type="bibr">2014</xref>; Hawkes and Keitt <xref rid="emi70430-bib-0023" ref-type="bibr">2015</xref>; Figure <xref rid="emi70430-fig-0002" ref-type="fig">2</xref>, Table <xref rid="emi70430-tbl-0002" ref-type="table">2</xref>). More generally, these findings are consistent with the concept of ecological memory, whereby past disturbances leave persistent imprints on community structure that shape subsequent responses to environmental change (Johnstone et al. <xref rid="emi70430-bib-0026" ref-type="bibr">2016</xref>).</p><p>Overall beta‐diversity (Aitchison distance) was also affected by the disturbance treatments, and the effect of the major pulse over time varied with disturbance history, as hypothesized (Table <xref rid="emi70430-supitem-0001" ref-type="supplementary-material">S2</xref>). However, because multivariate dispersion differed among treatments, these PERMANOVA effects may reflect differences in group centroids, dispersion, or both (Table <xref rid="emi70430-supitem-0001" ref-type="supplementary-material">S3</xref>). Moreover, dissimilarity among replicate communities within a treatment increased over time and null model analyses showed that this dissimilarity was associated with increased inferred stochasticity in community assembly (Figure <xref rid="emi70430-fig-0005" ref-type="fig">5</xref>), indicating a strong influence of stochasticity under dispersal limitation, which is in line with previous research (Chase <xref rid="emi70430-bib-0012" ref-type="bibr">2007</xref>; Zhou et al. <xref rid="emi70430-bib-0057" ref-type="bibr">2014</xref>; Vellend et al. <xref rid="emi70430-bib-0054" ref-type="bibr">2014</xref>; Le Moigne et al. <xref rid="emi70430-bib-0029" ref-type="bibr">2023</xref>; Figures <xref rid="emi70430-fig-0003" ref-type="fig">3</xref> and <xref rid="emi70430-fig-0004" ref-type="fig">4</xref>). Increased divergence among replicate communities indicates reduced predictability of community trajectories under identical environmental conditions. Contrary to our expectation (Figure <xref rid="emi70430-fig-0001" ref-type="fig">1b</xref>), divergence among replicates was not temporarily halted during the series of minor pulses. Before the major pulse, pairwise Aitchison distances increased more steeply in both the long and short recovery treatments than in the undisturbed control (Figure <xref rid="emi70430-fig-0004" ref-type="fig">4</xref>; Table <xref rid="emi70430-tbl-0002" ref-type="table">2</xref>), so the minor pulses accelerated rather than constrained divergence. This is consistent with the null model results discussed below, and suggests that repeated minor disturbances weakened deterministic filtering instead of imposing a common selective trajectory on replicate communities.</p><p>We expected selection to dominate under disturbance and stochasticity to become more influential under stable conditions, in the absence of disturbance (Vellend <xref rid="emi70430-bib-0052" ref-type="bibr">2010</xref>; Dini‐Andreote et al. <xref rid="emi70430-bib-0016" ref-type="bibr">2015</xref>; Zhou and Ning <xref rid="emi70430-bib-0059" ref-type="bibr">2017</xref>; Albright et al. <xref rid="emi70430-bib-0003" ref-type="bibr">2019</xref>). After the major pulse dissimilarity between replicates depended on disturbance history (Table <xref rid="emi70430-tbl-0002" ref-type="table">2</xref>). Most importantly, however, in both treatments with a disturbance history (long and short recovery), dissimilarity among replicates was higher in treatments receiving the major pulse, which was not the case in treatments without a disturbance history (Figure <xref rid="emi70430-fig-0004" ref-type="fig">4</xref>). Further, NST values were also higher in the long recovery treatment receiving the major pulse (Figure <xref rid="emi70430-fig-0005" ref-type="fig">5</xref>, Table <xref rid="emi70430-tbl-0002" ref-type="table">2</xref>). NST values should be interpreted comparatively within the context of this experimental system rather than as absolute indicators of deterministic versus stochastic assembly, because null model outcomes depend on the structure of the input data and model assumptions. The short recovery treatment was not associated with any significant difference between pulse treatments, though the trend was similar. Altogether, these results suggest that a history of disturbances can decrease the role of determinism caused by a later disturbance in community assembly, and, thereby, increase the relative contribution of stochasticity. Repeated minor salinity pulses may have pre‐filtered the community, which might have reduced fitness differences at the time of the major pulse and weakened selection, thereby increasing the relative influence of stochastic processes (Vellend <xref rid="emi70430-bib-0052" ref-type="bibr">2010</xref>; Chase and Myers <xref rid="emi70430-bib-0013" ref-type="bibr">2011</xref>; Nemergut et al. <xref rid="emi70430-bib-0034" ref-type="bibr">2013</xref>). Repeated minor disturbances may also have selectively removed highly sensitive taxa prior to the major pulse, leaving communities composed of taxa with more similar stress tolerances and competitive capacities. Under such conditions, fitness differences during the major pulse may become reduced, weakening deterministic environmental filtering and increasing the relative influence of stochastic processes such as drift and priority effects.</p><p>Although, as reported above, a number of studies have used microbial communities to investigate the role of disturbances for stochasticity and the role of repeated disturbances for community resistance, resilience and composition, few have investigated the role of repeated disturbances for stochasticity, as we did here. Exceptions are the studies by Santillan et al. (<xref rid="emi70430-bib-0044" ref-type="bibr">2019</xref>) and Santillan and Wuertz (<xref rid="emi70430-bib-0045" ref-type="bibr">2022</xref>), who exposed activated sludge communities to repeated disturbances of different frequency and found the strongest role of stochasticity for community assembly at intermediate disturbance frequency when also the highest alpha‐diversity was observed. These results bear similarities to our findings where the communities with a disturbance history showed the highest alpha‐diversity as well as stochastic assembly following the major disturbance. Future work should investigate how different combinations of disturbance frequency, intensity and recovery duration interact to shape the balance between deterministic and stochastic assembly across microbial systems. More broadly, our results suggest that microbial responses to disturbance cannot be fully understood from disturbance intensity alone, but depend critically on the sequence and timing of prior environmental exposures. When interpreting these findings, it is important to acknowledge potential methodological limitations. The large number of samples (<italic>n</italic> = 624) constrained the achievable sequencing depth per sample. Alpha‐diversity measures are strongly dependent on sequencing depth. However, it has been shown that robust trends in alpha‐diversity among samples can be obtained at lower sequencing depths than applied here (Lundin et al. <xref rid="emi70430-bib-0062" ref-type="bibr">2012</xref>). Further, rarefaction curves indicated that our sequencing depth captured the majority of the common taxa in each sample (Figure <xref rid="emi70430-supitem-0001" ref-type="supplementary-material">S1</xref>). However, detection of very rare taxa could have been limited, which can influence metrics sensitive to low‐abundance features, such as Aitchison distances and null model approaches. Increases in richness could also be understood as changes in the number of ASVs being above the detection limit rather than true changes in richness considering that the experiment was not open to recruitment by immigration, being performed in a closed system.</p><p>In our experiment, microbial communities were subject to dispersal limitation. If we had left replicates open to new dispersal during the experiment, we hypothesize that the importance of drift might have been smaller (Evans et al. <xref rid="emi70430-bib-0017" ref-type="bibr">2017</xref>; Fodelianakis et al. <xref rid="emi70430-bib-0018" ref-type="bibr">2021</xref>; Le Moigne et al. <xref rid="emi70430-bib-0029" ref-type="bibr">2023</xref>). In natural systems, immigration, spatial heterogeneity and trophic interactions may modify these dynamics, potentially dampening or amplifying the role of stochastic assembly observed here. Future studies could, thus, include the effects of dispersal in experiments addressing the roles of disturbance and disturbance history because these factors combined may influence metaecosystem resilience (Angeler et al. <xref rid="emi70430-bib-0007" ref-type="bibr">2023</xref>). However, on the other hand, the usefulness of both open and closed systems in experiments of this kind, for example for applications in biotechnology, has also been stressed (Santillan et al. <xref rid="emi70430-bib-0043" ref-type="bibr">2025</xref>).</p></sec><sec id="emi70430-sec-0013" disp-level="1"><label>5.</label><title>Conclusion</title><p>In summary, the unique time series of community samples in this study allowed us to closely follow community change in response to a series of salinity disturbances and a major disturbance event. Together, our findings demonstrate that bacterial community responses to disturbance are not only determined by the immediate stress but also by their disturbance history and recovery dynamics. Recent disturbances generate a short‐term ecological memory that enhanced richness, whereas longer intervals weakened this buffering effect. Additionally, a subsequent pulse increased inferred stochasticity in treatments with disturbance histories.</p></sec><sec id="emi70430-sec-0019" disp-level="1"><title>Author Contributions</title><p>

/Applications/ideas/1103_boundary_discovery/runs/learn_20261104_community/stages/01_materials/attempt-002/workspace/sources/shade_2012_fulltext.html:71:<meta name="citation_abstract" content="Microbial communities are at the heart of all ecosystems, and yet microbial community behavior in disturbed environments remains difficult to measure and predict. Understanding the drivers of microbial community stability, including resistance (insensitivity to disturbance) and resilience (the rate of recovery after disturbance) is important for predicting community response to disturbance. Here, we provide an overview of the concepts of stability that are relevant for microbial communities. First, we highlight insights from ecology that are useful for defining and measuring stability. To determine whether general disturbance responses exist for microbial communities, we next examine representative studies from the literature that investigated community responses to press (long-term) and pulse (short-term) disturbances in a variety of habitats. Then we discuss the biological features of individual microorganisms, of microbial populations, and of microbial communities that may govern overall community stability. We conclude with thoughts about the unique insights that systems perspectives - informed by meta-omics data- may provide about microbial community stability. ">

Understanding the drivers of microbial community stability, including resistance (insensitivity to disturbance) and resilience (the rate of recovery after disturbance) is important for predicting community response to disturbance. Here, we provide an overview of the concepts of stability that are relevant for microbial communities. First, we highlight insights from ecology that are useful for defining and measuring stability. To determine whether general disturbance responses exist for microbial communities, we next examine representative studies from the literature that investigated community responses to press (long-term) and pulse (short-term) disturbances in a variety of habitats. Then we discuss the biological features of individual microorganisms, of microbial populations, and of microbial communities that may govern overall community stability. We conclude with thoughts about the unique insights that systems perspectives – informed by meta-omics data – may provide about microbial community stability.</p><!--]--></div><!----><!--[--><div id="h2"><!--[--><h2>Introduction</h2><p>In habitats as diverse as soil and the human body, key ecosystem processes are driven by microbial communities – local assemblages of microorganisms that interact with each other and their environment (Konopka, <a href="#B79" class="ArticleReference" data-event="dt_articles-click-open_reference"><!--[--><!--]--><!--[-->2009<!--]--></a>). Thus, microbiology research in biomedical, environmental, agricultural, and bioenergy contexts shares a common challenge: to predict how functions and composition of microbial communities respond to disturbances (Robinson et al., <a href="#B121" class="ArticleReference" data-event="dt_articles-click-open_reference"><!--[--><!--]--><!--[-->2010a<!--]--></a>; Gonzalez et al., <a href="#B57" class="ArticleReference" data-event="dt_articles-click-open_reference"><!--[--><!--]--><!--[-->2011a<!--]--></a>,<a href="#B58" class="ArticleReference" data-event="dt_articles-click-open_reference"><!--[--><!--]--><!--[-->b<!--]--></a>; Costello et al., <span role="button" tabindex="0" id="B25-button" class="ArticleReference" data-event="dt_articles-click-open_reference"><!--[--><span id="B25a" class="ArticleReference__scrollTarget" aria-hidden="true"></span><!--]--><!--[-->2012<!--]--></span>).</p><p>Here, we introduce a breadth of topics that provide insight into the responses of microbial communities to disturbance. We first highlight key concepts from ecology that are useful in thinking about microbial stability, pointing readers to an extensive literature on the subject of disturbance and community stability. We then summarize the current state of knowledge about resistance and resilience of microbial communities inhabiting a variety of ecosystems, emphasizing overarching trends gleaned from a review of 247 representative studies. We next provide a synthesis of the properties of individual microorganisms, populations, and communities that influence microbial community stability. Finally, we discuss insights into stability that may emerge from a systems-level perspective – describing microbial communities as networks of genes, transcripts, proteins, and metabolite signals.</p><!--]--></div><div id="h3"><!--[--><h2>Key Concepts from Ecology</h2><!--[--><!--[--><!--]--><!--[--><h3>Defining disturbance</h3><!--]--><!--[--><!--]--><!--[--><p>Disturbances are causal events that either (1) alter the immediate environment and have possible repercussions for a community or (2) directly alter a community (Rykiel, <a href="#B125" class="ArticleReference" data-event="dt_articles-click-open_reference"><!--[--><!--]--><!--[-->1985<!--]--></a>; Glasby and Underwood, <a href="#B56" class="ArticleReference" data-event="dt_articles-click-open_reference"><!--[--><!--]--><!--[-->1996<!--]--></a>). After disturbance, community members may die (mortality) or change in their relative abundances (Rykiel, <a href="#B125" class="ArticleReference" data-event="dt_articles-click-open_reference"><!--[--><!--]--><!--[-->1985<!--]--></a>). A disturbance can be difficult to define, as its definition depends on scale and context. Disturbances occur at various spatial and temporal scales (Paine et al., <a href="#B109" class="ArticleReference" data-event="dt_articles-click-open_reference"><!--[--><!--]--><!--[-->1998<!--]--></a>) with different frequencies (number of occurrences per unit time), intensities (magnitude of the disturbance), extents (proportion of the ecosystem affected), and periodicities (regularity of occurrences; Grimm and Wissel, <a href="#B62" class="ArticleReference" data-event="dt_articles-click-open_reference"><!--[--><!--]--><!--[-->1997<!--]--></a>). Disturbances may also be defined relative to the disturbance regime of an ecosystem, such as a fire or flooding cycle.</p><!--]--><!--[--><!--]--><!--[--><p>Disturbances are often classified as <!--[--><i>pulses</i><!--]--> or <!--[--><i>presses</i><!--]--> depending on their duration (Bender et al., <span role="button" tabindex="0" id="B11-button" class="ArticleReference" data-event="dt_articles-click-open_reference"><!--[--><!--]--><!--[-->1984<!--]--></span>). In general, pulse disturbances are relatively discrete, short-term events, whereas presses are long-term or continuous (Figure <a href="#F1" class="ArticleReference" data-event="dt_articles-click-open_reference"><!--[--><!--]--><!--[-->1<!--]--></a>). However, these time scales may differ depending on the generation time of the community of interest. For instance, a tree falling in a forest may create a press disturbance to the underlying soil microorganisms, whereas the same event might be considered a pulse disturbance to nearby understory vegetation. Though the distinction between pulse and press disturbances has received much attention in the ecology literature, there is less discussion of patterns of microbial community responses to pulses and presses. However, microbial community responses to pulses and presses are important to consider in the context of global climate change. With global changes, pulse disturbances (e.g., extreme weather events) are expected to increase in frequency, and ongoing press disturbances are expected to continue (e.g., atmospheric increases in carbon dioxide, ocean acidification; Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change, <a href="#B67" class="ArticleReference" data-event="dt_articles-click-open_reference"><!--[--><!--]--><!--[-->2007<!--]--></a>). Therefore, throughout this work, we discuss microbial community responses in both pulse and press disturbance scenarios.</p><!--]--><!--[--><!--]--><div class="ArticleFigure" id="F1"><div A parameter is “recovered” when it is statistically indistinguishable from the pre-disturbance mean. Alternatively, the parameter may not recover and instead may stabilize at a new mean value representing an alternative stable state. This possibility is more likely in response to a press disturbance. Further, RS and RL could be related to normalized parameters describing the disturbance (e.g., intensity, duration, frequency of the stressor in relation to the pre-disturbance mean and variance), which is useful for cross-system comparisons.</p><!--]--><!--]--></figcaption></figure></button></div><!--[--><!--]--><!--]--><!--[--><!--[--><!--]--><!--[--><h3>Defining stability</h3><!--]--><!--[--><!--]--><!--[--><p>Disturbance and community stability are necessarily related, as stability is defined as a community’s response to disturbance (Rykiel, <a href="#B125" class="ArticleReference" data-event="dt_articles-click-open_reference"><!--[--><!--]--><!--[-->1985<!--]--></a>). Here, we adopt definitions most similar to Pimm (<a href="#B114" class="ArticleReference" data-event="dt_articles-click-open_reference"><!--[--><!--]--><!--[-->1984<!--]--></a>), in which stability is comprised of resistance and resilience (Table <a href="#T1" class="ArticleReference" data-event="dt_articles-click-open_reference"><!--[--><!--]--><!--[-->1<!--]--></a>), two quantifiable metrics that are useful for comparing community disturbance responses and have precedent in the microbial ecology literature (e.g., Allison and Martiny, <span role="button" tabindex="0" id="B2-button" class="ArticleReference" data-event="dt_articles-click-open_reference"><!--[--><!--]--><!--[-->2008<!--]--></span>). However, readers should be aware that the ecology literature includes many definitions of stability, and a full examination of these definitions is available elsewhere (Grimm and Wissel, <a href="#B62" class="ArticleReference" data-event="dt_articles-click-open_reference"><!--[--><!--]--><!--[-->1997<!--]--></a>). Here, resistance is defined as the degree to which a community is insensitive to a disturbance, and resilience is the rate at which a community returns to a pre-disturbance condition (Pimm, <a href="#B114" class="ArticleReference" data-event="dt_articles-click-open_reference"><!--[--><!--]--><!--[-->1984<!--]--></a>). A related concept, sensitivity, is the inverse of resistance and defined as the degree of community change following a disturbance. Both resistance and resilience are usually quantified in relation to a community’s level of intrinsic variability, sometimes referred to as the “normal operating range” (van Straalen, <a href="#B156" class="ArticleReference" data-event="dt_articles-click-open_reference"><!--[--><!--]--><!--[-->2002<!--]--></a>). There are many methods in the literature [see a recent summary by Griffiths and Philippot (<a href="#B59" class="ArticleReference" data-event="dt_articles-click-open_reference"><!--[--><!--]--><!--[-->2012<!--]--></a>)] for comparing resistance or resilience across communities (Orwin and Wardle, <a href="#B108" class="ArticleReference" data-event="dt_articles-click-open_reference"><!--[--><!--]--><!--[-->2004<!--]--></a>).</p><!--]--><!--[--><!--]--><div class="ArticleTable" id="T1"><div data-event="dt_articles-click-open_reference"><!--[--><!--]--><!--[-->2009<!--]--></a>)</td><!--]--><!--[--><!--]--></tr><!--]--><!--[--><!--]--><!--[--><tr><!--[--><!--]--><!--[--><td align="left">Metacommunity</td><!--]--><!--[--><!--]--><!--[--><td align="left">Within a regional landscape, a set of local communities whose members are linked by dispersal (Wilson, <a href="#B164" class="ArticleReference" data-event="dt_articles-click-open_reference"><!--[--><!--]--><!--[-->1992<!--]--></a>; Logue et al., <a href="#B96" class="ArticleReference" data-event="dt_articles-click-open_reference"><!--[--><!--]--><!--[-->2011<!--]--></a>)</td><!--]--><!--[--><!--]--></tr><!--]--><!--[--><!--]--><!--[--><tr><!--[--><!--]--><!--[--><td colspan="2" align="left" style="background-color:DarkGray;"><!--[--><!--]--><!--[--><b>COMMUNITY RESPONSE TERMS</b><!--]--><!--[--><!--]--></td><!--]--><!--[--><!--]--></tr><!--]--><!--[--><!--]--><!--[--><tr><!--[--><!--]--><!--[--><td align="left">Stability</td><!--]--><!--[--><!--]--><!--[--><td align="left">The tendency of a community to return to a mean condition after a disturbance (Pimm, <a href="#B114" class="ArticleReference" data-event="dt_articles-click-open_reference"><!--[--><!--]--><!--[-->1984<!--]--></a>); includes the components of resistance and resilience</td><!--]--><!--[--><!--]--></tr><!--]--><!--[--><!--]--><!--[--><tr><!--[--><!--]--><!--[--><td align="left"></td><!--]--><!--[--><!--]--><!--[--><td align="left">Ecological stability can be measured in many ways, including the persistence of populations through time, constancy of ecological attributes through time, resistance to a disturbance, or resilience after a disturbance (Worm and Duffy, <a href="#B168" class="ArticleReference" data-event="dt_articles-click-open_reference"><!--[--><!--]--><!--[-->2003<!--]--></a>)</td><!--]--><!--[--><!--]--></tr><!--]--><!--[--><!--]--><!--[--><tr><!--[--><!--]--><!--[--><td align="left">Resistance</td><!--]--><!--[--><!--]--><!--[--><td align="left">The degree to which a community withstands change in the face of disturbance (Pimm, <a href="#B114" class="ArticleReference" data-event="dt_articles-click-open_reference"><!--[--><!--]--><!--[-->1984<!--]--></a>; Allison and Martiny, <span role="button" tabindex="0" id="B2-button" class="ArticleReference" data-event="dt_articles-click-open_reference"><!--[--><!--]--><!--[-->2008<!--]--></span>). Inverse of <!--[--><i>sensitivity</i><!--]--></td><!--]--><!--[--><!--]--></tr><!--]--><!--[--><!--]--><!--[--><tr><!--[--><!--]--><!--[--><td align="left">Sensitivity</td><!--]--><!--[--><!--]--><!--[--><td align="left">The degree to which a community changes in response to disturbance, the inverse of resistance</td><!--]--><!--[--><!--]--></tr><!--]--><!--[--><!--]--><!--[--><tr><!--[--><!--]--><!--[--><td align="left">Resilience</td><!--]--><!--[--><!--]--><!--[--><td align="left">The rate at which a microbial community returns to its original composition after being disturbed (Allison and Martiny, <span role="button" tabindex="0" id="B2-button" class="ArticleReference" data-event="dt_articles-click-open_reference"><!--[--><!--]--><!--[-->2008<!--]--></span>). Commonly referred to as community recovery. Inverse of return time</td><!--]--><!--[--><!--]--></tr><!--]--><!--[--><!--]--><!--[--><tr><!--[--><!--]--><!--[--><td colspan="2" align="left" style="background-color:DarkGray;"><!--[--><!--]--><!--[--><b>COMMUNITY OUTCOMES</b><!--]--><!--[--><!--]--></td><!--]--><!--[--><!--]--></tr><!--]--><!--[--><!--]--><!--[--><tr><!--[--><!--]--><!--[--><td align="left">Stable state</td><!--]--><!--[--><!--]--><!--[--><td align="left">A condition where a community returns to its original composition or function following a disturbance (Beisner et al., <span role="button" tabindex="0" id="B10-button" class="ArticleReference" data-event="dt_articles-click-open_reference"><!--[--><span id="B10a" class="ArticleReference__scrollTarget" aria-hidden="true"></span><!--]--><!--[-->2003<!--]--></span>). Also known as community equilibrium or an attractor</td><!--]--><!--[--><!--]--></tr><!--]--><!--[--><!--]--><!--[--><tr><!--[--><!--]--><!--[--><td align="left">Alternative stable state</td><!--]--><!--[--><!--]--><!--[--><td align="left">A condition where a community moves to a different but stable composition or function following a disturbance. One of multiple, non-transitory stable states in which a community can exist (Beisner et al., <span role="button" tabindex="0" id="B10-button" class="ArticleReference" data-event="dt_articles-click-open_reference"><!--[--><span id="B10a" class="ArticleReference__scrollTarget" aria-hidden="true"></span><!--]--><!--[-->2003<!--]--></span>)</td><!--]--><!--[--><!--]--></tr><!--]--><!--[--><!--]--><!--[--><tr><!--[--><!--]--><!--[--><td align="left">Regime shift</td><!--]--><!--[--><!--]--><!--[--><td align="left">A large change in community composition arising from a shift between alternative stable states (Scheffer and Carpenter, <a href="#B127" class="ArticleReference" data-event="dt_articles-click-open_reference"><!--[--><!--]--><!--[-->2003<!--]--></a>)</td><!--]--><!--[--><!--]--></tr><!--]--><!--[--><!--]--></tbody><!--]--></table></div><div class="ArticleTable__description"><!--[--><p><!--[--><!--]--><!--[--><b>Common terms for disturbances, community responses, and community outcomes</b><!--]-->.</p><!--]--></div><div class="ArticleTable__foot"><!--[--><!--]--></div></div><!--[--><!--]--><!--[--><p>A community’s stability can be investigated in terms of functional or compositional parameters. In microbial ecology, many studies also focus on the degree to which functional and compositional stability are related. This may depend in large part on the particular function of interest (Schimel, <a href="#B128" class="ArticleReference" data-event="dt_articles-click-open_reference"><!--[--><!--]--><!--[-->1995<!--]--></a>). For functions that are carried out by many taxa (Schimel, <a href="#B128" class="ArticleReference" data-event="dt_articles-click-open_reference"><!--[--><!--]--><!--[-->1995<!--]--></a>), i.e., communities harboring a high degree of functional redundancy, changes in community composition may not correspond with changes in functional rates (Allison and Martiny, <span role="button" tabindex="0" id="B2-button" class="ArticleReference" data-event="dt_articles-click-open_reference"><!--[--><!--]--><!--[-->2008<!--]--></span>). Alternatively, for functions performed by only a few taxa (for example, in situations of ecological coherence of closely related taxa, Philippot et al., <a href="#B113" class="ArticleReference" data-event="dt_articles-click-open_reference"><!--[--><!--]--><!--[-->2010<!--]--></a>), the sensitivity and resilience of this function may closely follow changes in the abundance of those taxa. Notably, estimates of resistance and resilience for the same microbial community may have different values depending on whether compositional or functional responses are measured and on which functions are used to assess stability.</p><!--]--><!--[--><!--]--><!--[--><p>One perspective of stability, sometimes referred to as “ecological resilience,” relies on the existence of many stable states in which a community may reside (e.g., Holling, <a href="#B64" class="ArticleReference" data-event="dt_articles-click-open_reference"><!--[--><!--]--><!--[-->1973<!--]--></a>, <a href="#B63" class="ArticleReference" data-event="dt_articles-click-open_reference"><!--[--><!--]--><!--[-->1996<!--]--></a>; Botton et al., <span role="button" tabindex="0" id="B14-button" class="ArticleReference" data-event="dt_articles-click-open_reference"><!--[--><span id="B14a" class="ArticleReference__scrollTarget" aria-hidden="true"></span><!--]--><!--[-->2006<!--]--></span>). For instance, a community may shift to a new stable state when subjected to a press disturbance (Figure <a href="#F1" class="ArticleReference" data-event="dt_articles-click-open_reference"><!--[--><!--]--><!--[-->1<!--]--></a>). The existence of multiple equilibria can also be illustrated by the concept of a stability landscape (Beisner et al., <span role="button" tabindex="0" id="B10-button" class="ArticleReference" data-event="dt_articles-click-open_reference"><!--[--><span id="B10a" class="ArticleReference__scrollTarget" aria-hidden="true"></span><!--]--><!--[-->2003<!--]--></span>; Scheffer and Carpenter, <a href="#B127" class="ArticleReference" data-event="dt_articles-click-open_reference"><!--[--><!--]--><!--[-->2003<!--]--></a>; Collie et al., <span role="button" tabindex="0" id="B24-button" class="ArticleReference" data-event="dt_articles-click-open_reference"><!--[--><span id="B24a" class="ArticleReference__scrollTarget" aria-hidden="true"></span><!--]--><!--[-->2004<!--]--></span>; Folke et al., <a href="#B48" class="ArticleReference" data-event="dt_articles-click-open_reference"><!--[--><!--]--><!--[-->2004<!--]--></a>), which can be used to conceptualize microbial community responses to disturbance (Blodau and Knorr, <span role="button" tabindex="0" id="B12-button" class="ArticleReference" data-event="dt_articles-click-open_reference"><!--[--><!--]--><!--[-->2006<!--]--></span>; Mao-Jones et al., <a href="#B99" class="ArticleReference" data-event="dt_articles-click-open_reference"><!--[--><!--]--><!--[-->2010<!--]--></a>; Bürgmann et al., <span role="button" tabindex="0" id="B16-button" class="ArticleReference" data-event="dt_articles-click-open_reference"><!--[--><span id="B16a" class="ArticleReference__scrollTarget" aria-hidden="true"></span><!--]--><!--[-->2011<!--]--></span>; Seto and Iwasa, <a href="#B130" class="ArticleReference" data-event="dt_articles-click-open_reference"><!--[--><!--]--><!--[-->2011<!--]--></a>). In a visualization of a stability landscape, a ball represents a community that can exist in one of many different equilibrium states (basins) within the stability landscape (Beisner et al., <span role="button" tabindex="0" id="B10-button" class="ArticleReference" data-event="dt_articles-click-open_reference"><!--[--><span id="B10a" class="ArticleReference__scrollTarget" aria-hidden="true"></span><!--]--><!--[-->2003<!--]--></span>; Scheffer and Carpenter, <a href="#B127" class="ArticleReference" data-event="dt_articles-click-open_reference"><!--[--><!--]--><!--[-->2003<!--]--></a>; Figure <a href="#F2" class="ArticleReference" data-event="dt_articles-click-open_reference"><!--[--><!--]--><!--[-->2<!--]--></a>). A disturbance event is analogous to applying a force to the ball within its basin. A community may resist the disturbance, which is represented by the ball remaining in its basin. Alternatively, the community could change but exhibit resilience, which is represented by the ball moving outward from the basin but then returning to its original location (Figure <a href="#F2" class="ArticleReference" data-event="dt_articles-click-open_reference"><!--[--><!--]--><!--[-->2<!--]--></a>A). If resistance and resilience are low or the disturbance strong enough, the community may shift to an alternative equilibrium (also called alternative stable state), represented by the ball moving into a new basin. Once in an alternative equilibrium, the community’s return to the previous composition or function may be difficult (Botton et al., <span role="button" tabindex="0" id="B14-button" class="ArticleReference" data-event="dt_articles-click-open_reference"><!--[--><span id="B14a" class="ArticleReference__scrollTarget" aria-hidden="true"></span><!--]--><!--[-->2006<!--]--></span>). Moreover, environmental conditions shape the stability landscape (Figure <a href="#F2" class="ArticleReference" data-event="dt_articles-click-open_reference"><!--[--><!--]--><!--[-->2<!--]--></a>B). Thus, if a press disturbance permanently alters the stability landscape, this will have implications for community stability and the likelihood of community shifts to alternative stable states.</p><!--]--><!--[--><!--]--><div class="ArticleFigure" id="F2"><div class="ArticleFigure__header"><p class="ArticleFigure__title">Figure 2</p><button data-tootip-position="top center" Here, changes in community composition are assessed using axis scores from an ordination (e.g., principal coordinates analysis (PCoA) of Bray–Curtis similarities) before <!--[--><b>(A)</b><!--]--> and after <!--[--><b>(B)</b><!--]--> environmental change. The overlay “terrain” of the landscape shows the different stable states as basins, and the community is represented as a ball that is either maintained in its original basin or displaced to a new basin after a disturbance. Community resilience is represented by the slope of the basin walls, showing a rate of return to the original stable state.</p><!--]--><!--]--></figcaption></figure></button></div><!--[--><!--]--><!--[--><p>Studies of alternative stable states and regime shifts in microbial systems remain rare (Botton et al., <span role="button" tabindex="0" id="B14-button" class="ArticleReference" data-event="dt_articles-click-open_reference"><!--[--><span id="B14a" class="ArticleReference__scrollTarget" aria-hidden="true"></span><!--]--><!--[-->2006<!--]--></span>), though the conceptual framework is gaining popularity, especially among researchers interested in the human gut microbiome (Lozupone et al., <a href="#B98" class="ArticleReference" data-event="dt_articles-click-open_reference"><!--[--><!--]--><!--[-->2012<!--]--></a>), as the existence of alternative stable states may provide explanation as to the immense variability observed within and among individual gut microbial communities. There is also evidence of alternative stable states in the vaginal microbiome, where eight “super-groups” of distinct microbial assemblages have been detected across hundreds of healthy women (Zhou et al., <a href="#B171" class="ArticleReference" data-event="dt_articles-click-open_reference"><!--[--><!--]--><!--[-->2007<!--]--></a>). Additionally, there are a few concrete examples of microbial communities that exhibited regime shifts. For instance, increased influx of groundwater triggered a functional regime shift from iron-reduction to sulfate-reduction in anoxic sediments of mine drainage lakes (Blodau and Knorr, <span role="button" tabindex="0" id="B12-button" class="ArticleReference" data-event="dt_articles-click-open_reference"><!--[--><!--]--><!--[-->2006<!--]--></span>), and operational changes triggered a compositional and functional regime shift in a sequencing batch reactor for nitrogen elimination from urine (Bürgmann et al., <span role="button" tabindex="0" id="B16-button" class="ArticleReference" data-event="dt_articles-click-open_reference"><!--[--><span id="B16a" class="ArticleReference__scrollTarget" aria-hidden="true"></span><!--]--><!--[-->2011<!--]--></span>). Furthermore, regime shifts in microbial communities may have far-reaching consequences for ecosystems, as suggested by theoretical models of coral reef microbial communities that shift composition from antibiotic-producers to pathogens (Mao-Jones et al., <a href="#B99" class="ArticleReference" data-event="dt_articles-click-open_reference"><!--[--><!--]--><!--[-->2010<!--]--></a>). As time series studies are extended to include more disturbance events, alternative stable states may be detected for other microbial communities. In the example in Figure <a href="#F2" class="ArticleReference" data-event="dt_articles-click-open_reference"><!--[--><!--]--><!--[-->2<!--]--></a>, microbial community composition and function are mapped using multivariate ordination to visualize a stability landscape.</p><!--]--><!--[--><!--]--><!--]--><!--[--><!--[--><!--]--><!--[--><h3>Measuring stability: Community response to disturbance</h3><!--]--><!--[--><!--]--><!--[--><p>Ecologists have long considered how to quantify resistance and resilience of communities and their functions. One experimental design that specifically addresses the impact of a disturbance is “before-after-control-impact” (BACI; Stewart-Oaten et al., <a href="#B143" class="ArticleReference" data-event="dt_articles-click-open_reference"><!--[--><!--]--><!--[-->1992<!--]--></a>; Smith et al., <a href="#B138" class="ArticleReference" data-event="dt_articles-click-open_reference"><!--[--><!--]--><!--[-->1993<!--]--></a>; Ellis and Schneider, <span role="button" tabindex="0" id="B37-button" class="ArticleReference" data-event="dt_articles-click-open_reference"><!--[--><span id="B37a" class="ArticleReference__scrollTarget" aria-hidden="true"></span><!--]--><!--[-->1997<!--]--></span>; Stewart-Oaten and Bence, <a href="#B142" class="ArticleReference" data-event="dt_articles-click-open_reference"><!--[--><!--]--><!--[-->2001<!--]--></a>; Fraterrigo and Rusak, <a href="#B49" class="ArticleReference" data-event="dt_articles-click-open_reference"><!--[--><!--]--><!--[-->2008<!--]--></a>). But, BACI has known limitations [discussed in Underwood (<a href="#B151" class="ArticleReference" data-event="dt_articles-click-open_reference"><!--[--><!--]--><!--[-->1994<!--]--></a>)], including violation of assumptions of non-independence of samples collected over time. Thus, multivariate autoregressive moving-average models, which remove temporal autocorrelation, have been applied to understand the contribution of species and environmental interactions to the stability of communities (e.g., Ives et al., <a href="#B69" class="ArticleReference" data-event="dt_articles-click-open_reference"><!--[--><!--]--><!--[-->2003<!--]--></a>). Additionally, Bayesian approaches such as dynamic linear models (DLM) account for the autocorrelation of time series data, and estimate the sensitivity of data to disturbance (e.g., Carpenter and Brock, <span role="button" tabindex="0" id="B19-button" class="ArticleReference" data-event="dt_articles-click-open_reference"><!--[--><span id="B19a" class="ArticleReference__scrollTarget" aria-hidden="true"></span><!--]--><!--[-->2006<!--]--></span>). Techniques such as DLM also make projections about future behavior of a response variable based on pre-disturbance data distribution (sometimes called intervention). There are many other techniques that quantify temporal variability to assess the impact of disturbance and measure resilience (e.g., Underwood, <a href="#B151" class="ArticleReference" data-event="dt_articles-click-open_reference"><!--[--><!--]--><!--[-->1994<!--]--></a>; Ives, <a href="#B68" class="ArticleReference" data-event="dt_articles-click-open_reference"><!--[--><!--]--><!--[-->1995<!--]--></a>; Ives et al., <a href="#B70" class="ArticleReference" data-event="dt_articles-click-open_reference"><!--[--><!--]--><!--[-->2000<!--]--></a>; Fraterrigo and Rusak, <a href="#B49" class="ArticleReference" data-event="dt_articles-click-open_reference"><!--[--><!--]--><!--[-->2008<!--]--></a>). Methods for handling temporal datasets (e.g., Lennon, <a href="#B87" class="ArticleReference" data-event="dt_articles-click-open_reference"><!--[--><!--]--><!--[-->2011<!--]--></a>) will become increasingly useful to microbiologists as more and longer time series of microbial communities become available. However, the species-rich nature of many microbial datasets, especially those generated using high-throughput sequencing, present computational challenges that will likely require new methods of statistical analysis (Gonzalez et al., <a href="#B57" class="ArticleReference" data-event="dt_articles-click-open_reference"><!--[--><!--]--><!--[-->2011a<!--]--></a>).</p><!--]--><!--[--><!--]--><!--[--><p>When measuring stability, it is important to distinguish between responses to pulse and press disturbances, as recovery may be quantified by slightly different methods (Glasby and Underwood, <a href="#B56" class="ArticleReference" data-event="dt_articles-click-open_reference"><!--[--><!--]--><!--[-->1996<!--]--></a>). Ideally, resilience to a press disturbance should be determined after the community composition or function reaches its maximum deviation from the expected mean (Figure <a href="#F1" class="ArticleReference" data-event="dt_articles-click-open_reference"><!--[--><!--]--><!--[-->1<!--]--></a>). With a press, there is often more uncertainty about when the disturbance has caused the maximal change in the community, especially if it is unknown when the press disturbance began and whether it has ceased. Therefore, when to establish the baseline for measuring resilience after a press disturbance is less obvious, and therefore a major research challenge. By contrast, response to a pulse can be defined immediately after the pulse ends, although there may be a time lag before the disturbance response is completed.</p><!--]--><!--[--><!--]--><!--[--><p>Additionally, experimental settings allow pulse and press responses to be compared directly and described relative to one another. For example, tropical soil microbial communities exposed to fluctuating (pulse) anoxic-to-oxygenic conditions were compared to those exposed to continuous (press) anoxic or oxygenic conditions (DeAngelis et al., <span role="button" tabindex="0" id="B30-button" class="ArticleReference" data-event="dt_articles-click-open_reference"><!--[--><span id="B30a" class="ArticleReference__scrollTarget" aria-hidden="true"></span><!--]--><!--[-->2010<!--]--></span>). This pulse-press comparison revealed that communities exposed to repeated redox fluctuations were more diverse and more active (assessed by their RNA to DNA ratio) than communities exposed to a constant condition. Furthermore, when microbial communities are monitored long-term, pulse and press responses also may be compared <!--[--><i>post hoc</i><!--]-->. In these cases, community stability could serve as an indicator of unmeasured or unobserved pulse and press disturbances: short-term variability around a baseline (equilibrium) may be a sign of pulses while gradual shifts in the baseline may be a sign of presses (Shade et al., <a href="#B135" class="ArticleReference" data-event="dt_articles-click-open_reference"><!--[--><!--]--><!--[-->2012<!--]--></a>).</p><!--]--><!--[--><!--]--><!--]--><!--[--><!--[--><!--]--><!--[--><h3>Community invasibility as an indicator of stability</h3><!--]--><!--[--><!--]--><!--[--><p>Invasion, the successful establishment of a non-native organism in a community (Litchman, <a href="#B93" class="ArticleReference" data-event="dt_articles-click-open_reference"><!--[--><!--]--><!--[-->2010<!--]--></a>), can provide an indicator for both compositional and functional stability. Invasion is unique in that it can be considered both a cause and consequence of disturbance. In studies of communities with larger organisms, a well-known consequence of community disturbance is reduced resistance to invasion by alien species (called “niche opportunity”; Shea and Chesson, <a href="#B136" class="ArticleReference" data-event="dt_articles-click-open_reference"><!--[--><!--]--><!--[-->2002<!--]--></a>), but its parallel use as a functional indicator of stability in microbial communities has been limited, with a few exceptions (e.g., Robinson et al., <a href="#B122" class="ArticleReference" data-event="dt_articles-click-open_reference"><!--[--><!--]--><!--[-->2010b<!--]--></a>). Community invasion does, however, have a long history in microbial ecology in the context of agricultural inoculants and veterinary and clinical probiotics. For example, a century ago, Ilya Metchnikoff explored invasion of his own gut microbiome by lactobacilli consumed in sour milk, and found that the lactobacilli did not invade his gut community and needed to be replenished frequently to obtain the salubrious effects on his health that he reported (Metchnikoff, <a href="#B102" class="ArticleReference" data-event="dt_articles-click-open_reference"><!--[--><!--]--><!--[-->1908<!--]--></a>; Schmalstieg and Goldman, <a href="#B129" class="ArticleReference" data-event="dt_articles-click-open_reference"><!--[--><!--]--><!--[-->2008<!--]--></a>). A century of study of probiotics revealed the challenge of establishing new strains of bacteria in the mammalian gut, with many studies documenting disappearance of introduced strains within hours of entrance into the gastrointestinal tracts of pigs (e.g., Gardiner et al., <a href="#B52" class="ArticleReference" data-event="dt_articles-click-open_reference"><!--[--><!--]--><!--[-->2004<!--]--></a>) and humans (Robins-Browne and Levine, <a href="#B120" class="ArticleReference" data-event="dt_articles-click-open_reference"><!--[--><!--]--><!--[-->1981<!--]--></a>; Ventura and Perozzi, <a href="#B157" class="ArticleReference" data-event="dt_articles-click-open_reference"><!--[--><!--]--><!--[-->2011<!--]--></a>). These studies contributed to the broadly held sense that microbial communities are resistant to invasion, embodied in the concept of “colonization resistance” of the human microbiome (Savage, <a href="#B126" class="ArticleReference" data-event="dt_articles-click-open_reference"><!--[--><!--]--><!--[-->1977<!--]--></a>; Hopkins and Macfarlane, <a href="#B65" class="ArticleReference" data-event="dt_articles-click-open_reference"><!--[--><!--]--><!--[-->2003<!--]--></a>; Johnson-Henry et al., <a href="#B71" class="ArticleReference" data-event="dt_articles-click-open_reference"><!--[--><!--]--><!--[-->2008<!--]--></a>; Britton and Young, <span role="button" tabindex="0" id="B15-button" class="ArticleReference" data-event="dt_articles-click-open_reference"><!--[--><!--]--><!--[-->2012<!--]--></span>).</p><!--]--><!--[--><!--]--><!--]--><!--]--></div><div id="h4"><!--[--><h2>Knowns and Unknowns about Microbial Community Stability: An Updated Investigation of the Literature Considering Responses to Pulse and Press Disturbances</h2><p>Recent studies have reported that, in general, soil microbial communities are not resistant to disturbances, as measured by composition, and that even within several years many communities fail to recover entirely (Allison and Martiny, <span role="button" tabindex="0" id="B2-button" class="ArticleReference" data-event="dt_articles-click-open_reference"><!--[--><!--]--><!--[-->2008<!--]--></span>). To extend this analysis to non-soil communities, we explored the literature for studies investigating microbial community stability in the face of disturbance (see <a href="#A1" class="ArticleReference" data-event="dt_articles-click-open_reference"><!--[--><!--]--><!--[-->Appendix<!--]--></a>). We considered 247 studies, and these studies included a total of 378 investigations of soil, marine and freshwater, engineered (e.g., wastewater treatment, bioreactors), and host-associated (gut) systems to discern patterns of stability that may be broadly applicable to microbial communities. From this exploration, we chose representative examples from the literature to illustrate key points, as our search was not intended to be exhaustive. We focused our comparisons on microbial community responses to pulse and press disturbances.</p><p>Investigations of microbial community stability generally fell into two broad classes: <!--[--><i>observations</i><!--]-->, which typically involved <!--[--><i>in situ</i><!--]-->, large-scale disturbances (e.g., deforestation, typhoons, temperature changes), and <!--[--><i>designed experiments</i><!--]--> that usually involved small-scale disturbances (e.g., nutrient amendment, temperature alterations, or fumigation, Figure <a href="#F3" class="ArticleReference" data-event="dt_articles-click-open_reference"><!--[--><!--]--><!--[-->3<!--]--></a>A). Resistance and resilience were assessed either based on microbial community composition or function (Allison and Martiny, <span role="button" tabindex="0" id="B2-button" class="ArticleReference" data-event="dt_articles-click-open_reference"><!--[--><!--]--><!--[-->2008<!--]--></span>; Little et al., <a href="#B95" class="ArticleReference" data-event="dt_articles-click-open_reference"><!--[--><!--]--><!--[-->2008<!--]--></a>), which are sometimes linked (Balvanera et al., <span role="button" tabindex="0" id="B8-button" class="ArticleReference" data-event="dt_articles-click-open_reference"><!--[--><span id="B8a" class="ArticleReference__scrollTarget" aria-hidden="true"></span><!--]--><!--[-->2006<!--]--></span>; Cardinale et al., <span role="button" tabindex="0" id="B18-button" class="ArticleReference" data-event="dt_articles-click-open_reference"><!--[--><span id="B18a" class="ArticleReference__scrollTarget" aria-hidden="true"></span><!--]--><!--[-->2006<!--]--></span>). Many studies (23%) measured only microbial composition, assessed by multivariate analysis of molecular fingerprints or 16S rRNA gene sequences, as the response variable to assess stability. Some studies (18%) measured community functions (respiration, biomass production, or activity of extracellular enzymes). Finally, a large number of studies (58%) measured both community composition and function.</p><div class="ArticleFigure" id="F3"><div class="ArticleFigure__header"><p loading="lazy"></picture><figcaption><!--[--><!--[--><p><!--[--><!--]--><!--[--><b>Summary of a literature survey of microbial community responses to pulse and press disturbances</b><!--]-->. The survey included studies that investigated changes in microbial community structure after biological, chemical, or physical disturbances. <!--[--><b>(A)</b><!--]--> Representation of investigations across ecosystem types, and by whether the investigation was a designed experiment or opportune <!--[--><i>in situ</i><!--]--> observations after a disturbance. There were 378 total investigations from 247 total studies, as some studies investigated more than one disturbance or measured more than one function, and some studies did not report either. <!--[--><b>(B)</b><!--]--> Resistance was determined by sensitivity (change in composition or function after disturbance). Some investigations measured both composition and function, and were included in both charts. <!--[--><b>(C)</b><!--]--> If a community was sensitive to disturbance, resilience was measured as recovery to pre-disturbance composition or function. Many investigations that reported community sensitivity did not assess recovery.</p><!--]--><!--]--></figcaption></figure></button></div><p>From our examination of 310 experimental and 68 observational investigations of microbial responses to disturbances, 82% reported sensitivity to disturbance, either in composition (26%), function (21%), or both (35%, Figure <a href="#F3" class="ArticleReference" data-event="dt_articles-click-open_reference"><!--[--><!--]--><!--[-->3<!--]--></a>B). This is in agreement with previous findings for soil communities (Allison and Martiny, <span role="button" tabindex="0" id="B2-button" class="ArticleReference" data-event="dt_articles-click-open_reference"><!--[--><!--]--><!--[-->2008<!--]--></span>), and suggests that most microbial communities may be sensitive to disturbances. One caveat to this finding is that it may be more difficult to publish results of experiments in which communities did not change when challenged with a disturbance, and so this finding may reflect a potential bias in the literature. A habitat-by-habitat summary of sensitivity to disturbance is given in Figures <a href="#FA1" class="ArticleReference" data-event="dt_articles-click-open_reference"><!--[--><!--]--><!--[-->A1<!--]--></a>A,B in Appendix. Though we considered microbial communities from many habitats, soil communities were most represented, affirming that the majority of disturbance investigations in microbial ecology are from soil habitats.</p><p>Only a few investigations explicitly measured resilience (Figure <a href="#F3" class="ArticleReference" data-event="dt_articles-click-open_reference"><!--[--><!--]--><!--[-->3<!--]--></a>C). Of those 148 investigations that reported community sensitivity to disturbance and also examined recovery, only a small fraction reported return to pre-disturbance composition (13%), function (8%), or both (2%). However, it was unclear whether resilience was not observed in some investigations because of biases in sampling intensity or duration after the disturbance (Figure <a href="#FA2" class="ArticleReference" data-event="dt_articles-click-open_reference"><!--[--><!--]--><!--[-->A2<!--]--></a> in Appendix) or because the communities were not, in fact, resilient. The normal variability of microbial communities in the absence of any disturbance event was also often unreported. Without <!--[--><i>a priori</i><!--]--> knowledge of community turnover, it may be difficult to inform post-disturbance sampling intensity or duration. Thus, knowledge of baseline microbial community stability as well as post-disturbance dynamics remains limited for many habitats and contexts.</p><p>Our results suggest that microbial communities are equally sensitive to pulse and press disturbances (Figure <a href="#F3" class="ArticleReference" data-event="dt_articles-click-open_reference"><!--[--><!--]--><!--[-->3<!--]--></a>B). Drawing on the subset of investigations that assessed resilience, our results hint that microbial communities may be more resilient after pulse disturbances than after press disturbances (Figure <a href="#F3" class="ArticleReference" data-event="dt_articles-click-open_reference"><!--[--><!--]--><!--[-->3<!--]--></a>C). Recovery from pulse disturbances was reported more often for microbial community function than for composition, while recovery from press disturbances was approximately the same for both function and composition. As more disturbance studies become available, further work will be needed to compare resilience quantitatively across press and pulse disturbances, as different disturbance types (chemical, biological, physical, combination) were differently represented within pulse and press investigations (Figures <a href="#FA1" class="ArticleReference" data-event="dt_articles-click-open_reference"><!--[--><!--]--><!--[-->A1<!--]--></a>C,D in Appendix). For example, though physical disturbance types were represented approximately equally in both pulse and press investigations, press disturbances included a larger representation of chemical disturbance types than pulse.</p><p>Additionally, the literature survey results draw attention to our current knowledge gaps regarding microbial community responses to pulse and press disturbances. Specifically, there is limited understanding of microbial responses to biological pulse disturbances and to disturbance combinations for both pulses and presses. First, investigations of microbial responses to biological disturbance types were rare, especially in pulse disturbance scenarios (Figures <a href="#FA1" class="ArticleReference" data-event="dt_articles-click-open_reference"><!--[--><!--]--><!--[-->A1<!--]--></a>C,D in Appendix). Examples of pulse biological disturbances include phytoplankton blooms, which not only impact neighboring microbial communities but also have implications for both heterotrophic and autotrophic contributions to global carbon cycling (e.g., Teeling et al., <a href="#B146" class="ArticleReference" data-event="dt_articles-click-open_reference"><!--[--><!--]--><!--[-->2012<!--]--></a>). Therefore, understanding pulse biological disturbances remains an important gap to fill. Second, investigations of disturbance combinations were also uncommon among the literature surveyed, though pulse disturbances included a larger representation of disturbance combinations than press (Figures <a href="#FA1" class="ArticleReference" data-event="dt_articles-click-open_reference"><!--[--><!--]--><!--[-->A1<!--]--></a>C,D in Appendix). Compounded disturbances include those that occur simultaneously or within the recovery time of a preceding disturbance. Because compounded disturbances may lead to regime shifts (e.g., Paine et al., <a href="#B109" class="ArticleReference" data-event="dt_articles-click-open_reference"><!--[--><!--]--><!--[-->1998<!--]--></a>), studying microbial community responses to compounded disturbances is increasingly important in face of global climate change.</p><p>It is interesting that though many studies measured functional responses (63%), there has been limited conceptual development on the role of pulse and press disturbances in driving relationships between microbial community composition and function. The presence of functionally redundant species in microbial communities has been suggested to increase functional resilience (e.g., Allison and Martiny, <span role="button" tabindex="0" id="B2-button" class="ArticleReference" data-event="dt_articles-click-open_reference"><!--[--><!--]--><!--[-->2008<!--]--></span>); however, the degree of functional redundancy among microorganisms remains controversial. Diversity – function relationships could be probed by asking whether press and pulse disturbances select for different community memberships (see <a href="#s1" class="ArticleReference" data-event="dt_articles-click-open_reference"><!--[--><!--]--><!--[-->Biological Features That Contribute to Microbial Resistance and Resilience<!--]--></a>). Applying combinations of press and pulse disturbances to microbial communities could create gradients in community diversity that may clarify the role of disturbance in driving diversity-function relationships.</p><p>The results of our literature survey reveal that we have much to learn about the nature of change and recovery for microbial communities from many habitats. Conceptual progress across disciplinary boundaries within microbial ecology could be achieved by cross-system comparison of stability. However, we currently lack a common framework and standard format of reporting compositional and functional responses to disturbance, which inhibits more quantitative cross-system comparisons. There has been recent progress to standardize microbial community data in the new biological observation matrix (.biom taxa table; see <!--[--><a href="http://biom-format.org">biom-format.org</a><!--]-->), as used by concerted efforts to collect and curate large microbial datasets, such as by the Earth Microbiome Project (Gilbert et al., <a href="#B54" class="ArticleReference" data-event="dt_articles-click-open_reference"><!--[--><!--]--><!--[-->2010<!--]--></a>). This and similar efforts will support development of disturbance theory for microbial ecology.</p><!--]--></div><div id="s1"><!--[--><h2>Biological Features that Contribute to Microbial Resistance and Resilience</h2><p>Survival of individual cells is a prerequisite for population-level persistence, which is a prerequisite for community-level recovery (Figure <a href="#F4" class="ArticleReference" data-event="dt_articles-click-open_reference"><!--[--><!--]--><!--[-->4<!--]--></a>). In this section, we explicitly focus on compositional, taxon-based resistance and resilience, but make connections to functional resistance and resilience where possible. We hypothesize that there are biological attributes that are of greater importance for microbial community resistance and resilience under pulse disturbance scenarios (orange circles, Figure <a href="#F4" class="ArticleReference" data-event="dt_articles-click-open_reference"><!--[--><!--]--><!--[-->4<!--]--></a>), while other attributes are generally important for both pulse and press disturbances (purple circles).</p><div class="ArticleFigure" id="F4"><div class="ArticleFigure__header"><p class="ArticleFigure__title">Figure 4</p><button data-tootip-position="top center"
